title: Quantization sensitivity & rollout roadmap - Optimize walkthrough
summary: Workshop-style walkthrough of Redwood Optimize quant profiles, INT8 vs FP8 sensitivity on clinical extraction workload, and a proposed pilot/rollout roadmap. Customer cares about latency SLOs, deterministic quality, SOC 2 requirements, and ability to run in VPC/private infra.
action_items: Maya: Send tailored pilot terms and pricing sheet (includes burst capacity) by 2026-03-10
Diego: Share sample quantization runbook + recommended qprofiles for our clinical NER workload by 2026-03-09
Evan (Customer): Provide 2 representative eval prompt sets (short triage + long report extraction) by 2026-03-09
Priya (Customer): Confirm VPC peering window and firewall requirements by 2026-03-12
next_steps: Run INT8 sensitivity sweep on their long-report eval set (Redwood + BlueWave) next week
Schedule a 60-min canary roll demo once initial qprofile completes
Share security docs (SOC2, encryption, KMS integration) and an on-prem checklist
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. We're gonna run through Optimize quant profiles, do a few practical tradeoff examples with INT8 and FP8, and build a small rollout roadmap for your pilot. Quick intros?
[00:18] Sasha Patel: Sasha here, CTO at BlueWave. Focused on clinical NLP pipelines, mostly extraction from discharge summaries. Latency needs are pretty tight for triage flows.
[00:31] Evan Moore: Evan, ML eng. I own the models and evaluation. We have a distilled LLM and some ops to run.
[00:37] Priya Singh: Priya, DevOps. I'll handle networking and certs, also the VPC notes.
[00:41] Noah Lee: Noah, security. Looking at compliance, audit logs, key mgmt.
[00:44] Diego Rios: Diego, SE at Redwood. I'll jump into the qprofile examples and the console.
[00:48] Maya: Great. Quick framing — most customers want the cheapest configuration that keeps quality within a fidelity threshold. Today we'll show how Optimize suggests profiles, what the console tells you about latency vs quality, and how canaries/rollbacks work.
[01:05] Sasha: Important: we cannot accept quality regressions on core entities — patient identifiers, medication names. Even small hallucinations are blockers.
[01:15] Maya: Understood. We'll focus on specificity-sensitive metrics. Diego, can you pull up the console?
[01:23] Diego: Yep. Pulling the Optimize tab — this is a mock of the BlueWave workload we imported earlier, two eval sets: triage short prompts (avg 24 tokens) and long-report extraction (avg 780 tokens). You'll see baseline metrics on hosted FP16 and an INT8 candidate.
[01:43] Diego: Note — the console's "fidelity" metric is a composite: entity F1 weighted heavily, plus an answer-level exact match for key fields. It's configurable per customer.
[01:53] Evan: Is that composite something we define? Can we upweight meds?
[01:57] Diego: Yes you can. In the eval config you pick entity groups and weightings. We recommended meds and patient id be 0.5 of the score.
[02:06] Sasha: Perfect. For compliance, Noah needs to see how logs look.
[02:10] Noah: Specifically audit trails for model version, qprofile, and who triggered rollbacks.
[02:15] Maya: Redwood stores per-request model metadata and exposes audit logs to your SIEM via S3 hooks or syslog. We'll attach the SOC2 docs after.
[02:25] Noah: Also KMS — we use GCP KMS, want HSM-backed keys later.
[02:29] Diego: We support KMS/HSM integrations; there are some config steps for private deployments — we'll include a checklist.
[02:36] Maya: Ok demo time. I'm going to show two runs: an INT8 qprofile that reduces token cost ~3.4x and an FP8 candidate that reduces 2.1x but has different latency behavior on long sequences.
[02:50] Diego: Starting the sweep now. Note the console will run N samples and generate per-sample delta to baseline.
[03:00] Diego: First observation — INT8 gives lower throughput on very short prompts due to kernel startup overhead, but it shines on batched long sequences.
[03:12] Evan: That matches our op logs — triage has short 30–50 token prompts, long-extracts are multi-hundred tokens.
[03:20] Diego: Right. Here's a chart — x axis is avg seq len, y axis is relative latency. For triage, FP16 baseline is 70ms, INT8 is 110ms, FP8 is 65ms. For 800-token reports baseline is 1.4s, INT8 is 0.9s, FP8 1.1s.
[03:38] Sasha: So INT8 penalizes short prompts. That's concerning for triage.
[03:42] Maya: This is where smart routing comes in — you can route triage to FP16 or FP8 variant and long-report to INT8. Redwood Optimize can suggest split ratios based on your traffic distribution.
[03:56] Priya: Can routing happen in VPC/private infra?
[03:59] Diego: Yes, same policy layer works in Private. The control plane issues route decisions, but you can also bake rules into the local router for air-gapped setups.
[04:10] Evan: On quality — how do you compare hallucination rates? Are we running BLEU-like or specific NER F1?
[04:16] Diego: For this workflow we use NER F1 and field exact-match. The console shows per-field deltas; you can set thresholds to block rollout if any critical field drops > 1.5%.
[04:26] Evan: Can we see a detailed per-entity diff?
[04:29] Diego: Yep — click into any sample and you'll get token-level diff with confidence bars. Note some mis-recognitions in the export: sometimes "KV cache" was transcribed as "k V cache" in our logs — ignore that, but the runtime keeps an exact KV trace.
[04:46] Sasha: About canaries — what's realistic window? We need deterministic rollback.
[04:51] Maya: We recommend a 24–72 hour canary depending on load. The canary is traffic-weighted; if fidelity drops or error rates spike, system can auto rollback. You can set guardrails (e.g., require 95% statistical confidence).
[05:03] Priya: Who triggers rollback? Auto only or manual?
[05:06] Diego: Both. You can enable auto rollback or require manual approval. We log the decision and preserve the canary traces for audit.
[05:14] Noah: That logging is mandatory for us. Need to ensure immutable logs for the roll events.
[05:18] Maya: We stream immutable events to your S3 with object locking if required. We'll include the architecture note.
[05:26] Sasha: Back to quality: show us a sample where INT8 fails and FP8 passes.
[05:30] Diego: Pulling sample #42 — long report. Baseline FP16 extracts "metoprolol" correctly, INT8 maps to "metaphorol" (misspell), FP8 maps correctly. The diff shows token-level probs dropped on suffixes.
[05:45] Evan: That suffix misspell is bad — for medication NER, a single char change could break downstream mapping to RxNorm.
[05:51] Maya: Right — we propose two mitigations: 1) constrained decoding/post-lexicon normalization for meds; 2) selective quantization where the final layers remain FP16/FP32 while bulk is INT8.
[06:03] Diego: This is called mixed-precision qprofile — we keep attention and final LM head in FP16. It recovers item-level fidelity but gives most of the cost win.
[06:12] Evan: Cost tradeoff numbers?
[06:14] Diego: Mixed-precision recovers 90% of fidelity lost by pure INT8 and retains ~2.6x token cost reduction vs baseline. Pure INT8 was ~3.4x.
[06:23] Sasha: So mixed-precision may be our default for meds.
[06:26] Maya: Exactly. The Optimize tool can auto-suggest which layers to exempt based on sensitivity sweeps.
[06:33] Priya: About throughput — if triage needs sub-200ms P99, can we meet that with routing?
[06:38] Diego: Yes, route triage to FP8 or FP16. FP8 gave the best latency on short prompts in our earlier chart. We can also pre-warm or reserve a tiny dedicated pool for triage on Redwood Dedicated or Private.
[06:50] Sasha: How does caching interact with quant profiles? If we cache prefixes, does INT8 still help?
[06:55] Diego: Good question. If you cache KV for common prefixes, INT8's benefits amplify because cache-lookups reduce compute. But you must ensure cache serialization is compatible across quant variants — Redwood handles canonical KV format and cross-variant compatibility in the runtime.
[07:10] Evan: If we do Private on-prem, are there kernel differences that change latency? We've heard Triton on our infra performed differently.
[07:18] Diego: Kernel selection varies by hardware; our compilation step picks optimized kernels per device and quant format. On certain old GPUs INT8 kernels may be suboptimal; Optimize flags that in the profile. We'll include a hardware compatibility matrix.
[07:30] Maya: Let's talk about pilot scope. Suggested pilot pillars: 1) Sensitivity sweep across eval sets, 2) Mixed-precision baseline and routing policy, 3) Canary for 2 weeks on 10% traffic, 4) Security review and VPC setup. Any objections?
[07:46] Sasha: Timeline?
[07:47] Maya: If we start next week, Diego runs sensitivity sweep (3–4 days), we deliver qprofile suggestions and a canary plan, then a two-week canary. So end-to-end ~4 weeks.
[07:59] Evan: Data sharing — do you need raw PII? We prefer synthetic or de-id sets.
[08:03] Diego: Use de-id or synthetic. For accurate fidelity you can provide a small redacted set with representative tokens. We have local masking guidance.
[08:13] Priya: For VPC peering we'll likely need one maintenance window. I can coordinate.
[08:17] Maya: Great. Quick live demo — I'm going to toggle a suggested qprofile into a staging canary.
[08:23] Diego: Applying profile now. Note the interface warns that this changes quant config for the model version. You can annotate the rollout note.
[08:32] Diego: Canary policy options: 10% traffic, 24 hours, evaluation checks every 10 minutes for entity F1 and response correctness.
[08:42] Evan: Can we add a strict block if medication exact match drops > 0.5%?
[08:47] Diego: Yes — set a per-field guard. I'll add that.
[08:50] Maya: While that runs, some Qs from Noah on encryption at rest: do we keep deduped logs? How long?
[08:55] Noah: For compliance we need 12 months audit retention, encrypted with our KMS key.
[08:59] Diego: We can mirror logs to your bucket with server-side encryption using your KMS ARN. Retention policy is configurable.
[09:06] Noah: Also SSO — we need SAML with SCIM sync for role-based access.
additional_transcript_part2:
[09:18] Maya: We'll include SAML/SCIM setup docs. Any more technical deep dives?
[09:25] Evan: One more — mixed-precision rollout on sequence lengths. Is the selection per-request or per-model?
[09:30] Diego: qprofiles are per-model version but routing can pick a model variant per-request. So you can have model:v1-int8-mixed and model:v1-fp8 and route dynamically.
[09:40] Sasha: What about cost forecasting? Can you simulate monthly bill given traffic shape?
[09:44] Diego: Yes — Optimize has a cost simulator where you feed hourly qps and split by prompt length; it projects token cost, compute, and burst surcharges. We'll run that with your traffic shape.
[09:56] Priya: Any known risks around deterministic outputs with FP8? We heard FP8 can be less stable.
[10:01] Maya: FP8 stability depends on model and quant scheme. For many models FP8 gives near-baseline fidelity and slightly improved latency on short prompts. We recommend sensitivity sweeps.
[10:12] Evan: Ok. To recap — we want: 1) Redwood runs INT8/FP8/mixed sweep on our two eval sets, 2) routing plan for triage vs long, 3) pilot canary plan, 4) security docs + VPC checklist.
[10:25] Maya: Perfect. We'll follow up with the pilot SOW and the pricing sheet.
[10:29] Sasha: Thanks all.
[10:31] Maya: Thanks, wrap up.
[10:33] [call ends]
